questions.stem: A 27 year old woman has felt low for 9 days since her relationship ended. She has lost interest in her running club, sleeps poorly and has phoned in sick twice. She has no thoughts of self-harm. She asks whether she has depression. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the minimum duration of symptoms needed before a depressive episode can be diagnosed?
questions.e: Depression needs persistent low mood or anhedonia with functional impairment for at least 2 weeks; at 9 days she does not yet meet criteria.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the minimum duration of symptoms needed before a depressive episode can be diagnosed?

clues: lost interest in her running club
steps.x: Low mood, anhedonia and impaired work function are all there, but the duration is under the threshold.

elim: Too short: a week of low mood after a stressor is not enough for a depressive episode.
Far longer than needed; depression can be diagnosed after 2 weeks of persistent symptoms.
Not the threshold; ICD and DSM use at least 2 weeks.
This is the time to continue antidepressants after recovery, not the diagnostic duration.

steps.x: At least 2 weeks of symptoms most of the day, nearly every day. Review her again rather than labelling it yet.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has 5 weeks of depressed mood and reduced energy. He still enjoys watching football with his son. He wakes at 4 am, has lost his appetite, cannot concentrate at work and feels guilty about letting his family down. He has no delusions or hallucinations and no suicidal thoughts.
questions.q: Which is the most likely ICD-10 severity of his depressive episode?
o: Severe depressive episode with psychotic features
Severe depressive episode without psychotic features
questions.e: ICD-10 moderate depression is 2 core symptoms plus at least 3 others; he has depressed mood and low energy with early waking, poor appetite, poor concentration and guilt.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely ICD-10 severity of his depressive episode?
Count the core symptoms (mood, interest, energy): he has 2. Then count the others: sleep, appetite, concentration, guilt.

elim: Mild is 2 core plus 2 others; he has 2 core plus 4 others.
He has no delusions or hallucinations.
Severe needs all 3 core symptoms; he still enjoys football, so interest is preserved.
He has 6 symptoms for over 2 weeks, well above threshold.

steps.x: 2 core + 3 or more others = moderate. Severe needs all 3 core symptoms.

questions.stem: A 36 year old teacher has 3 weeks of feeling low most of the day, nearly every day. She also has poor sleep, fatigue and poor concentration. Her appetite and self-esteem are normal and she has no thoughts of death. Her GP is applying the ICD-11 criteria for a depressive episode.
questions.q: Which is the minimum number of the 10 ICD-11 symptoms required for a diagnosis?
questions.e: ICD-11 needs at least 5 of 10 symptoms most of the day, nearly every day, for 2 weeks or more, including one affective symptom (low mood or anhedonia).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the minimum number of the 10 ICD-11 symptoms required for a diagnosis?

clues: 3 weeks of feeling low most of the day, nearly every day
poor sleep, fatigue and poor concentration
steps.x: She has 4 symptoms: low mood, poor sleep, fatigue and poor concentration. Duration is enough.

elim: Too few; ICD-11 needs 5, including an affective symptom.
Too few; she has 4 symptoms and still does not meet criteria.
This is what she has, which falls one short of the ICD-11 threshold.
More than needed; 5 is the cut-off.

steps.x: ICD-11: 5 of 10 symptoms for at least 2 weeks, one of them affective.

questions.stem: A 51 year old man has 6 weeks of poor appetite, early morning waking, poor concentration and agitation. His wife says he no longer gardens or plays golf, which he used to love, and sits watching television without interest. His temperature is 36.8°C and pulse rate 80 bpm.
questions.q: Which of his symptoms is a core (affective) symptom of depression?
o: Loss of interest in activities he used to enjoy
questions.e: The core symptoms are low mood and anhedonia; he has anhedonia, so at least one affective symptom is present.

steps.x: The question asks: Which of his symptoms is a core (affective) symptom of depression?

clues: no longer gardens or plays golf, which he used to love
steps.x: No longer enjoying things he used to love is anhedonia.

elim: A biological feature, highly suggestive but not a core symptom.
A biological feature, not a core symptom.
An associated symptom, not one of the core pair.
An associated feature, not a core symptom.

steps.x: Core = low mood and anhedonia. Everything else is biological or associated.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is brought by his wife with 2 months of low mood and loss of interest. He wakes at 4 am. On examination he sits still, speaks slowly and quietly with long pauses before answering, and makes little eye contact. He denies hallucinations. His TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on mental state examination?
questions.e: Slowed movement and speech with long response latency is psychomotor retardation, a recognised feature of depression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely finding on mental state examination?

clues: sits still, speaks slowly and quietly with long pauses before answering
steps.x: Slowed movement and speech in a man with depressive symptoms.

elim: Rapid jumping between ideas is a feature of mania.
Grandiosity suggests mania; depressive delusions are of guilt or worthlessness.
Rapid, hard-to-interrupt speech is mania, the opposite of his slow speech.
A first-rank symptom of schizophrenia, not depression.

steps.x: Depression can cause psychomotor retardation or agitation. Speed-up features point to mania.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has 2 months of low mood. She has stopped seeing friends and feels she is a burden to her husband. Her husband says their relationship has changed. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. Her FBC and TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which other symptom is most likely to be present?
o: Reduced need for sleep with high energy
questions.e: Reduced libido is a recognised symptom of depression alongside poor concentration and thoughts of death; the other options describe mania or organic disorders.

steps.x: The question asks: Which other symptom is most likely to be present?
Worthlessness plus a change in the relationship in a woman with low mood.

elim: A feature of mania or hypomania.
Characteristic of mania, not depression.
Pressured speech is a feature of mania.
Typical of delirium tremens or Lewy body dementia.

steps.x: Depressive symptoms include reduced libido, reduced concentration and recurrent thoughts of death.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man has 4 months of low mood, weight loss and early morning waking. For the last 2 weeks he has heard a voice telling him he is worthless and deserves to die. He has no history of psychosis, drugs or alcohol. His temperature is 36.7°C and pulse rate 84 bpm. Urine drug screen is negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A mood-congruent derogatory voice appearing after months of severe depression is psychotic depression, not a primary psychotic disorder.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: a voice telling him he is worthless and deserves to die
steps.x: The voice matches his mood and appeared well after the depression started.

elim: His urine drug screen is negative and he denies drug use.
He is low and slowed, not elated or overactive.
His hallucinations are mood-congruent and came after months of depression.
Needs psychotic symptoms as prominent as the mood symptoms; here they follow and match the depression.

steps.x: Severe depression plus mood-congruent delusions or hallucinations = psychotic depression.

questions.stem: A 42 year old man has depression after losing his job. He scores 19 on the PHQ-9. He lives with his wife and two young children, attends church weekly and has no firearms. Two years ago he took an overdose of paracetamol after an argument. He drinks 10 units of alcohol a week.
questions.q: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of suicide?
questions.e: A previous suicide attempt is among the strongest predictors of completed suicide; the other options are protective factors.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature of his history most increases his risk of suicide?
Separate the risk factors from the protective factors in the history.

elim: Religious and community involvement is a protective factor.
Lack of access to means lowers risk.
Living with a supportive partner is protective.
Responsibility for children is usually a protective factor.

steps.x: Suicide is the key complication. Previous attempts raise risk; family, faith and no access to means protect.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman's husband died 4 months ago. Her daughter is worried because she is still upset. She cries when she sees his photographs but enjoys visits from her grandchildren. She has a PHQ-9 score of 16, and her daughter is worried that she now has depression rather than grief.
questions.q: Which additional feature would most support a depressive episode rather than uncomplicated grief?
o: Crying when she sees his photographs
Feeling his presence in the house
Pervasive worthlessness and loss of interest in everything
questions.e: Grief comes in time-limited waves linked to reminders with preserved self-esteem; persistent pervasive low mood, anhedonia and worthlessness suggest depression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which additional feature would most support a depressive episode rather than uncomplicated grief?

clues: cries when she sees his photographs
steps.x: At the moment her sadness is triggered by reminders and she still enjoys things: that is grief.

elim: Distress triggered by reminders is typical of normal grief.
Sensing the deceased is common in normal bereavement.
Waves of sadness that come and go are the pattern of uncomplicated grief.
Longing for the deceased is a core feature of normal grief.

steps.x: Grief = waves tied to the loss. Depression = pervasive low mood, anhedonia and worthlessness.

questions.stem: A 78 year old man has become forgetful over 3 months since a fall. He is withdrawn, eats little and wakes at 3 am. On cognitive testing he answers 'I don't know' to most questions and complains loudly about his poor memory. His B12, TFTs and CT head are normal.
questions.q: Which feature would most support depressive pseudodementia rather than Alzheimer's disease?
o: Global memory loss affecting recent and remote memory equally
questions.e: Pseudodementia gives apparent global memory loss with 'don't know' answers and short onset; Alzheimer's begins with a short-term memory pattern.

steps.x: The question asks: Which feature would most support depressive pseudodementia rather than Alzheimer's disease?

clues: answers 'I don't know' to most questions
steps.x: Short history, early waking, poor appetite and 'don't know' answers point to depression mimicking dementia.

elim: Patients with true dementia tend to confabulate or hide deficits.
Suggests Lewy body dementia or delirium.
Typical of progressive Alzheimer's disease.
A slow insidious course fits true dementia; his history is 3 months.

steps.x: Severe depression can mimic dementia with apparent global memory loss. Treat the depression.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man with COPD was made redundant 3 months ago. For 7 weeks he has felt low, stopped going to his pub quiz and slept until noon. He feels worthless and cannot concentrate. He drinks 14 units a week, unchanged. His oxygen saturation is 94% breathing air. FBC and TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Low mood, anhedonia, hypersomnia, worthlessness and poor concentration for 7 weeks is a depressive episode; chronic illness and a life stressor commonly coexist.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
Chronic illness and redundancy are risk factors. Hypersomnia counts as a sleep disturbance.

elim: His alcohol intake is moderate and unchanged.
Persistent mild low mood needs 2 years, not 7 weeks.
His symptoms are low mood and anhedonia rather than worry.
Delirium is acute with fluctuating attention; his course is 7 weeks with normal bloods.

steps.x: Depression often coexists with chronic illness and stress; look for at least 2 weeks of core symptoms.

questions.stem: A 74 year old woman has 2 months of tiredness, poor sleep with waking at 4 am, and loss of interest in her church group. She feels her family would be better off without her but has no plans. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Normal baseline bloods rule out the organic mimics; anhedonia, early waking and thoughts of being a burden indicate a depressive episode.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: loss of interest in her church group
steps.x: Classic depressive features; the bloods are there to exclude the mimics.

elim: Her TSH and free T4 are normal.
Her haemoglobin and MCV are normal.
Her glucose is normal.
Her B12 is normal.

steps.x: Baseline FBC, TFTs, B12/folate and glucose exclude anaemia and hypothyroidism. Normal results support depression.

questions.stem: A 21 year old university student has 5 weeks of feeling low, loss of enjoyment in music, reduced appetite and poor concentration that has made him miss deadlines. He feels guilty about wasting his parents' money. He has never had a period of elevated mood. His pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Five weeks of low mood and anhedonia with biological symptoms, guilt and functional impairment and no prior highs is a depressive episode.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: never had a period of elevated mood
steps.x: Both core symptoms, over 2 weeks, with impaired study.

elim: Needs an episode of mania or hypomania; he has never had elevated mood.
Needs at least 2 years of alternating mild highs and lows.
Needs at least 2 years of persistent low mood.
His main symptoms are low mood and anhedonia, not excessive worry.

steps.x: Low mood + anhedonia + functional impairment for 2 weeks or more = depressive episode.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has 6 weeks of low mood, fatigue and poor concentration. She has heavy periods and has noticed some hair loss. Her pulse rate is 64 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. Her GP thinks she has depression but wants to exclude a physical cause first.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?
questions.e: Baseline FBC, TFTs, B12/folate and glucose exclude anaemia (heavy periods) and hypothyroidism (hair loss, fatigue), the key mimics of depression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial set of investigations?
Heavy periods suggest anaemia; hair loss and fatigue suggest hypothyroidism.

elim: Not indicated without focal neurology or red flags.
Not a routine screen for depression.
Only relevant if she is on lithium.
Does not exclude anaemia or hypothyroidism, which her history suggests.

steps.x: Before labelling depression, check FBC, TFTs, B12/folate and glucose.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has 1 month of low mood, anhedonia, poor sleep and guilt. He is struggling at work. He has no physical symptoms. His FBC and TFTs are normal. He asks which test will confirm whether he has depression.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
o: Clinical assessment of history and mental state
questions.e: Depression is diagnosed clinically from the history and mental state examination against ICD/DSM criteria; no blood test or scan confirms it.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
Physical causes are already excluded; he is asking for the confirmatory step.

elim: Imaging does not diagnose depression.
A research marker of HPA-axis dysfunction, not a diagnostic test.
Does not diagnose depression.
Not a valid or used test; depression is a clinical diagnosis.

steps.x: Gold standard = clinical assessment. Bloods only exclude mimics.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has 2 months of low mood, poor sleep and fatigue. She completes a PHQ-9 questionnaire at her GP surgery and scores 17. She has no suicidal thoughts. PHQ-9 (see item resources). She is still working but finds it a struggle. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which severity of depression does her PHQ-9 score indicate?
questions.e: A PHQ-9 of 15 to 19 is moderately severe; 17 falls in this band.

steps.x: The question asks: Which severity of depression does her PHQ-9 score indicate?
Place 17 on the PHQ-9 bands.

elim: Mild is 5 to 9.
Minimal is 0 to 4.
Moderate is 10 to 14.
Severe is 20 to 27.

steps.x: PHQ-9: 0-4 none, 5-9 mild, 10-14 moderate, 15-19 moderately severe, 20-27 severe.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man has 3 months of low mood, weight loss of 5 kg, poor concentration and recurrent thoughts that he would be better off dead. He has no plans. He scores 23 on the PHQ-9. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 132/82 mmHg. PHQ-9 (see item resources).
questions.q: Which severity of depression does his PHQ-9 score indicate?
questions.e: A PHQ-9 of 20 or more indicates severe depression, matching his weight loss and recurrent thoughts of death.

steps.x: The question asks: Which severity of depression does his PHQ-9 score indicate?

clues: recurrent thoughts that he would be better off dead
steps.x: 23 is above 20; his symptoms also include thoughts of death.

elim: Mild is 5 to 9.
Moderate is 10 to 14.
Moderately severe is 15 to 19.
None or minimal is 0 to 4.

steps.x: PHQ-9 20 to 27 = severe depression.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman has 3 months of severe low mood. For a week she has believed that her insides are rotting and that she is being punished for her sins. She is eating little but drinking fluids. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Her GP diagnoses psychotic depression.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Start sertraline and review in 4 weeks
Urgent referral to the specialist mental health crisis team
questions.e: Psychotic depression is a severe presentation with mood-congruent nihilistic and guilt delusions and needs urgent specialist input.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
Nihilistic and guilt delusions in severe depression.

elim: Low-intensity therapy is for mild depression, not psychosis.
Psychotic depression needs urgent specialist input.
Delays treatment of a severe illness.
Psychotic depression needs specialist care, often an antidepressant plus an antipsychotic or ECT.

steps.x: Psychotic depression = urgent specialist referral, not GP-only management.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man is diagnosed with moderate depression by his GP. When asked how he is coping, he says that sometimes he wishes he would not wake up. He lives alone and works night shifts. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Ask about suicidal plans, intent and access to means
Prescribe sertraline and review in 4 weeks
questions.e: The first step in managing depression is always risk: thoughts, plans, intent, access to means, previous attempts and protective factors.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: wishes he would not wake up
steps.x: Passive suicidal ideation in a man living alone.

elim: Unsafe before his risk has been assessed.
Risk must be assessed first, and under-30s need review at 1 week.
Treatment comes after deciding whether he is safe.
Bloods can wait; his immediate safety cannot.

steps.x: Every depression assessment includes a suicide risk assessment before treatment is planned.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 5 weeks of low mood, poor sleep and tiredness. She is still working. Her PHQ-9 score is 6. She has no suicidal thoughts and no history of mania. She would prefer not to take tablets. PHQ-9 (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: With a PHQ-9 below 16 (mild depression), first-line is low-intensity psychological therapy such as guided self-help or group CBT rather than medication.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
A score of 6 is mild, and she does not want tablets.

elim: Reserved for severe, life-threatening or treatment-resistant depression.
Medication is not first-line in mild depression.
Used for augmentation or bipolar disorder, not mild depression.
Antidepressants are not first-line for mild depression.

steps.x: Mild depression: low-intensity psychological therapy first, not drugs.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has 3 months of low mood, anhedonia and poor sleep. His PHQ-9 score is 18. He has completed a course of guided self-help without benefit and wants medication. He has no history of mania, no suicidal thoughts and no other medical problems.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
questions.e: For moderate depression an SSRI is the first-line drug, and sertraline is first choice (fluoxetine or citalopram are alternatives).

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate drug treatment?
Moderately severe depression, mania excluded, wants a drug.

elim: A tricyclic: more toxic in overdose and not first-line.
A benzodiazepine; it does not treat depression and causes dependence.
An augmenting agent or mood stabiliser, not first-line.
An SNRI used later, after an SSRI.

steps.x: First-line antidepressant = SSRI, with sertraline first choice.

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman has 6 weeks of low mood and her GP plans to start an SSRI. She mentions that last summer she slept 3 hours a night for a week, felt full of energy and spent £4000 on clothes. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most important consideration before prescribing an antidepressant?
o: She needs a baseline ECG for sertraline
questions.e: Her history suggests a hypomanic episode; antidepressants alone can precipitate mania in undiagnosed bipolar disorder, so screen for mania before prescribing.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most important consideration before prescribing an antidepressant?

clues: slept 3 hours a night for a week
steps.x: Reduced need for sleep, high energy and overspending is hypomania.

elim: Not the relevant risk in this history.
Not routinely needed for sertraline.
They are not; under-30s need early review at 1 week.
SSRIs take 2 to 4 weeks to work.

steps.x: Always screen for mania or hypomania before starting an antidepressant.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man has 4 months of severe low mood with anhedonia, early waking and weight loss. His PHQ-9 score is 22. He has no delusions, is eating and drinking, and has no suicidal plans. He has no history of mania. He has not had any treatment before.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
questions.e: NICE recommends combining CBT with an antidepressant in severe depression; ECT is reserved for life-threatening or resistant cases.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
Severe by PHQ-9 but not life-threatening, and untreated.

elim: For life-threatening or treatment-resistant depression; he is eating and has no plans.
Insufficient for severe depression.
Low-intensity therapy is for mild depression.
Severe depression needs active treatment.

steps.x: Severe depression: CBT plus an SSRI. ECT only if life-threatening or resistant.

questions.stem: A 38 year old woman started sertraline 50 mg for moderate depression 8 weeks ago. Her mood has barely improved. On questioning she says she takes it only 2 or 3 days a week because she forgets. She has no side effects or suicidal thoughts.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Review adherence and encourage daily dosing
questions.e: With a poor response, first review adherence, then optimise the dose, then switch or seek specialist help.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: takes it only 2 or 3 days a week
steps.x: The poor response is explained by missed doses.

elim: Augmentation is for resistant depression, not non-adherence.
She has not had an adequate trial of treatment.
Switching is premature when the drug has not been taken properly.
Same problem: no adequate trial yet.

steps.x: Poor response: check adherence, optimise dose, then switch or refer.

questions.stem: A 45 year old man started sertraline for moderate depression 4 months ago. For the last 6 weeks he has felt back to his normal self and his PHQ-9 is 3. He asks if he can stop the tablets now. He has no side effects.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue sertraline for 2 more weeks then stop
Continue sertraline for at least 6 months after recovery
questions.e: NICE advises continuing antidepressants for at least 6 months after remission to reduce relapse risk.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?

clues: felt back to his normal self
steps.x: He has recovered only 6 weeks ago.

elim: Too short; relapse risk is high.
Lifelong treatment is not needed after a first episode.
Stopping now raises relapse risk and may cause discontinuation symptoms.
There is no reason to switch.

steps.x: Continue antidepressants at least 6 months after recovery, then taper.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has taken fluoxetine 20 mg for 3 months for depression with little benefit despite good adherence. Her psychiatrist decides to switch her to sertraline. She has no suicidal thoughts. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to switch?
o: Add sertraline to fluoxetine and continue both
Start sertraline 200 mg the day after stopping fluoxetine
Stop fluoxetine and wait 6 months before starting sertraline
Stop fluoxetine today and start sertraline 50 mg today
Stop fluoxetine, wait 4 to 7 days, then start low-dose sertraline
questions.e: Fluoxetine has a long half-life, so it is withdrawn and a 4 to 7 day gap is left before starting a low dose of the new SSRI.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to switch?
Switching from fluoxetine, the SSRI with the longest half-life.

elim: Combining SSRIs risks serotonin syndrome.
Fluoxetine's long half-life means it lingers; start low after a gap.
Far too long a gap.
A direct switch is fine between shorter-acting SSRIs, not from fluoxetine.

steps.x: From fluoxetine: withdraw, gap of 4 to 7 days, start low dose of the new SSRI.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man has taken citalopram 20 mg for 10 weeks for moderate depression. He takes it daily but his mood is unchanged. His GP decides to change to sertraline. He has no history of mania. His ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to switch?
o: Leave a 4 to 7 day gap before starting sertraline
Stop citalopram and start sertraline the next day
Stop citalopram and wait 2 weeks before sertraline
Taper citalopram over 6 months before sertraline
questions.e: A direct switch is possible between citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline and paroxetine; only fluoxetine needs a washout gap.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate way to switch?
Switching between two shorter-acting SSRIs.

elim: Two SSRIs together risk serotonin syndrome.
This gap is needed when switching from fluoxetine, not citalopram.
An unnecessary gap that leaves him untreated.
Far too slow.

steps.x: Direct switch between citalopram, escitalopram, sertraline and paroxetine.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman started sertraline for moderate depression 5 days ago. She phones her GP because she feels more anxious and jittery and her mood is no better. She has no suicidal thoughts and no rash. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and temperature 36.7°C.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Continue sertraline; anxiety is common early and benefit takes 2 to 4 weeks
Stop sertraline because it has failed
questions.e: SSRIs can initially worsen anxiety and agitation and take 2 to 4 weeks to work, so she should be reassured and continue with review.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate advice?
Early activation in the first week, with no suicidal thoughts.

elim: Benzodiazepines cause dependence and are not a long-term answer.
Raising the dose early is likely to worsen activation.
It is too early to judge; SSRIs take 2 to 4 weeks.
Too early to switch; fluoxetine causes the same early activation.

steps.x: SSRIs take 2 to 4 weeks and can worsen anxiety early. Warn patients before starting.

questions.stem: A 47 year old man with moderate depression starts sertraline 50 mg today. He has no history of self-harm, no suicidal thoughts and no history of mania. He lives with his partner. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg.
questions.q: When is the most appropriate time for his first review?
questions.e: Patients over 30 with no increased risk are reviewed every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months; under-30s are seen at 1 week.

steps.x: The question asks: When is the most appropriate time for his first review?
Age over 30 with no added risk.

elim: Review at 1 week is for those under 30 or at higher suicide risk.
Too long; review every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months.
Far too long.
All patients starting an antidepressant need review.

steps.x: Under 30: review at 1 week. Over 30: every 2 to 4 weeks for the first 3 months.

questions.stem: A 60 year old woman has had severe depression for 2 years. She has had adequate trials of sertraline, mirtazapine and venlafaxine with lithium augmentation, and a full course of CBT, with no improvement. Her PHQ-9 is 24 and she is unable to work or care for herself.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: ECT is indicated for treatment-resistant depression and for severe episodes with marked functional impairment needing a rapid response.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most appropriate management?

clues: unable to work or care for herself
steps.x: Several drugs, augmentation and CBT have all failed.

elim: She has already had full CBT without benefit.
Far too low intensity for severe resistant depression.
She has already failed adequate trials of several drugs.
Another SSRI is unlikely to help after multiple failures.

steps.x: ECT: treatment-resistant depression, or severe life-threatening depression needing rapid response.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has 2 months of low mood. He falls asleep normally but wakes at 4 am every day and cannot get back to sleep. His mood is worst in the morning. He has lost his appetite and 4 kg in weight. His TFTs are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his early morning waking?
o: Disruption of circadian and HPA-axis rhythms
Excess dopamine in the mesolimbic pathway
questions.e: Early morning waking reflects disruption of circadian and HPA-axis rhythms and is characteristic of biological (melancholic) depression.

steps.x: The question asks: Which is the most likely mechanism of his early morning waking?

clues: mood is worst in the morning
steps.x: Early waking, diurnal mood variation and appetite loss: a biological depression.

elim: Associated with psychosis, not early waking.
His TFTs are normal.
Not suggested; he has a depressive picture.
Causes daytime sleepiness and snoring, not early waking with low mood.

steps.x: Early morning waking = disrupted circadian and HPA rhythms, a melancholic feature.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man has 3 months of severe low mood. He now believes he has committed terrible crimes and that he has no money, although his bank statements are normal. He has no previous psychiatric history. Before this episode his mood and thinking were normal.
questions.q: Which feature best distinguishes this presentation from a primary psychotic disorder?
o: He has first-rank symptoms such as thought broadcasting
He has negative symptoms for years before the low mood
His delusions began before his low mood
The delusions are bizarre and unrelated to mood
The delusions are mood-congruent and followed the depressive onset
